column6: The commentary joins firm weaving with the meeting of bones; Psalm 139 says the speaker’s bones were not hidden while he was intricately woven, bringing both bodily structure and weaving into one image.

column5: bones and sinews knit into a body
column6: The commentary treats the meeting of bones as a fitted joint; Job describes God clothing the speaker with skin and flesh and knitting him together with bones and sinews, a distinct image of bodily assembly.
The commentary names the meeting of bones as haqq; the first human recognizes the woman as bone of his bones, making shared bodily substance a kinship image rather than an anatomical junction.
The commentary says pieces are joined into a sound whole; Genesis describes two people clinging and becoming one flesh, a relational form of joining that adds kinship to the construction image.
The commentary defines repair as the opposite of corruption; Isaiah calls the restored people repairers of a breach and restorers of streets, making repair both structural and communal.

column5: heals broken hearts and binds wounds
column6: The commentary’s salih repairs what is spoiled; the Psalm depicts God healing broken hearts and binding wounds, applying repair directly to damaged persons.

column5: heals after tearing and binds after striking
column6: The commentary opposes repair to corruption; Hosea calls the people to return because the one who tore them will heal them and bind their wounds, making restoration follow damage.
The commentary says the good work repairs what is spoiled; Jeremiah’s potter reworks a marred vessel into another form, a concrete image of repair through reshaping.
The commentary makes mutual counsel join and strengthen separate parts; Proverbs says one person sharpens another as iron sharpens iron, a direct image of reciprocal strengthening.

The commentary says mutual advice connects pieces and haqq makes the weave firm; Colossians speaks of hearts knit together in love and reaching full assurance, linking cohesion with shared understanding.

column5: whole structure joined and growing into a temple
column6: The commentary fits parts into a secure structure; Ephesians describes the whole building being joined together and growing into a holy temple, an architectural image for a community.

The commentary says one piece is joined to another; in the Shepherd’s vision, stones fit together in the tower identified with the Church, giving that connection an early Christian communal interpretation.
The commentary stresses soundness and exact fit; Isaiah describes a tested cornerstone laid as a firm foundation, connecting reliable construction with trust.
The commentary’s fitted door and joined structure depend on a sound meeting point; the Psalm’s rejected stone becomes the head of the corner, making a once-discarded piece structurally decisive.

Jesus applies the rejected-stone saying to the builders’ judgment of him; this Christian reading of Psalm 118 makes the building image a reversal in which the rejected one becomes structurally central.

column5: Isaiah’s chosen cornerstone applied to Christ
column6: The commentary’s firm fit and foundation imagery meets Peter’s citation of Isaiah’s tested cornerstone as Christ, adding a Christian interpretation in which trust in the chosen stone prevents shame.

The commentary makes work place bricks and repair what is broken; James insists that faith without works is dead, directly pairing belief with enacted conduct while adding a distinct argument about their necessity.

column5: wise woman builds; folly tears down
column6: The commentary’s good work repairs and constructs; Proverbs contrasts a wise woman building her house with folly tearing it down, making the same household image express constructive and destructive conduct.
The commentary makes counsel join parts into a stable structure; Jesus says a house divided against itself cannot stand, giving disunity the opposite structural consequence.

The commentary’s builder and repairer produce a sound moral structure; Isaiah’s owner clears stones, plants a vineyard, and builds its tower, yet receives wild grapes, a crafted project whose result fails its purpose.

The commentary joins constructive action with haqq; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice and righteousness but found bloodshed and a cry, making failed ethical fruit the reversal of sound building.

column5: members care for one another without division
column6: The commentary makes counsel connect parts; Paul says the body should have no division and its members should have the same care for one another, giving bodily cohesion a reciprocal ethical consequence.

column5: חקק ~ ح ق ق; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
column6: Isaiah says Zion is engraved on God’s palms and her walls are continually before him; this possible root correspondence extends the commentary’s firm word and bodily-junction imagery to an enduring inscription, without establishing cognacy.

The commentary’s mutual counsel in truth resembles the command to reprove one’s neighbor; Arakhin discusses how difficult it is both to give and receive rebuke, making reciprocal correction a demanding practice rather than a simple formula.

column5: firm foundation paired with turning from iniquity
column6: The commentary opposes sound construction to a weak house and corruption; 2 Timothy says God’s firm foundation stands, then pairs its seal with the command to depart from iniquity, joining structural security to ethical conduct.
